title: Weigh yourself in a lift
hook: You stand on a scale in a lift and it lurches upward. Does your weight change?

knows: weight is mass times gravity, W = m g
doesNotKnow: that a scale reads the support force N from the floor, not gravity itself
that N changes whenever you accelerate up or down (N = m (g + a))

misconception: What a scale shows is a fixed property of you; a lift cannot change it.
objective: The learner can explain that a scale measures how hard the floor pushes, and that the floor must push harder than gravity to accelerate you upward: 70 x (9.81 + 2) = 827 N.

claims.text: A 70 kg person's weight (gravity's pull) is about 687 N, and it does not change when the lift moves.
claims.source: W = m g = 70 x 9.81 = 686.7 N with g = 9.81 m/s^2; the lift's motion does not change the Earth's pull (the lift moves a few metres, g changes negligibly).

claims.text: A scale reads the push of the floor on you (the normal force), not gravity's pull directly.
claims.source: A spring or strain-gauge scale measures the compressive force between you and the platform: the normal force (OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, section 6.1, worked example 'What Does the Bathroom Scale Read in an Elevator?').

claims.text: Accelerating upward at 2 m/s², the scale reads 70 × (9.81 + 2) = 827 N; accelerating downward at 2 m/s², 547 N.
claims.source: Second law for the person, up positive: N - m g = m a, so N = m (g + a): 826.7 N at a = +2, 546.7 N at a = -2 (artifacts/scratch/w4phys/check.mjs). Stage slider 0.5-4 m/s^2 gives 406.7-966.7 N.

claims.text: Riding at steady speed reads the same as standing still; 'accelerating up' includes slowing down on the way down.
claims.source: N depends on acceleration a, not velocity: a = 0 at any steady speed gives N = m g. A lift moving down and braking has an upward acceleration, so N > m g.

claims.text: Model: the person stands still relative to the lift and the scale reads instantly; g = 9.81 m/s².
claims.source: Idealisation stated in this record: no bouncing of the scale's spring, constant acceleration in each phase.

recall.question: A lift is moving down and braking to stop at the ground floor. Compared with standing still, a scale under you reads…
recall.why: Braking while going down is an upward acceleration, so the floor must push harder than gravity pulls: N = m(g + a) is more than m g.
